item.title: Airfares Have Spiked. Is the Death of Spirit Airlines to Blame?
item.description:
If you’ve shopped for airline tickets recently, you’ve likely experienced sticker shock. Airfares have been rising consistently over the past year, averaging 24 percent more in August than a year earlier, according to the Consumer Price Index.

Holiday fares are reaching new highs. The booking app Hopper said domestic fares were up 31 percent for Thanksgiving compared with last year’s.

“It’s the most expensive holiday travel season in a decade, and I can only say a decade because my data goes back a decade,” said Hayley Berg, an economist with Hopper, citing the high cost of jet fuel, which has spiked since the start of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran in February.

Before May, budget seekers could resort to a consistent source of low-cost fares: Spirit Airlines. But since the ultra-low-cost carrier shut down this spring, after declaring bankruptcy, airlines that once competed with Spirit have been released from the carrier’s downward pressure on prices.

Cirium, an aviation analytics company, found that fares on former Spirit routes had increased roughly 5 to 6 percent in June since the year before. Though the company cautioned that Spirit’s exit alone couldn’t be credited for the rise, it noted that on one route between Cleveland and Las Vegas, the average fare among eight competing carriers in that period rose to $272 from about $192, or more than 40 percent.

Here’s what to know about the impact of Spirit’s closure on fares and where to look for airline bargains.

Airfares are complex, influenced by demand as well as costs, such as fuel, and factors in the broader economy, including inflation, making it hard to quantify the loss of Spirit.

Cirium looked at 1,126 city pairs where Spirit flew in June 2025. More than 90 percent of fares on those routes climbed over the next year after the airline shut down; the median fare rose 25.3 percent.

The hardest-hit destinations, according to the online travel agency FlightHub, are Spirit’s former focus cities, including Detroit, Houston, Orlando, Fort Lauderdale, Las Vegas and New York, as well as leisure destinations such as Cancún.

In Detroit, for example, FlightHub looked at 42 routes that Spirit formerly flew and found that the median fares rose to $227 in summer 2026, after the airline’s closure, from $125 the summer before.

But price rises go beyond Spirit’s network. Cirium analyzed roughly 37,000 city pairs without a Spirit route and found that the median increase from June 2025 to this year was 18.3 percent.

“Several pressures landed at the same time,” David Krauter, the chief executive of Going.com, a service that finds cheap airfares, wrote in an email, noting the rise in costs for fuel and labor.

“Summer demand stayed strong, but airlines didn’t add many seats to keep up,” he added. “Then one of the country’s biggest low-cost carriers disappeared completely. Any one of those would push fares up. All of them together is what travelers are paying for now.”

In the absence of Spirit, a handful of ultra-low-cost carriers remain, including the Denver-based Frontier Airlines, which offers a mix of city and leisure destinations, including in Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean.

Another, Allegiant Air, based in Las Vegas, focuses on domestic nonstop flights.

Both carriers charge for things like carry-on and checked bags, seat assignments and in-flight refreshments. Fees range from $2.99 to board first on a Frontier flight to $80 for a seat selection on Allegiant.

A hybrid between low-cost and full-service carriers, Jet Blue Airways is strongest in the Eastern United States, especially in New York, Boston and Fort Lauderdale, with service to many other destinations in Florida and the Caribbean. It recently promoted flights from $200 round trip between New York and Fort Lauderdale, Fla.

Smaller airlines, such as Breeze Airways, tend to fly point-to-point from secondary airports. Breeze flies to more than 90 cities, including some in the Caribbean and Latin America. Another small carrier, Avelo Airlines, concentrates its service on the East Coast between Connecticut and Florida.

Sun Country Airlines operates from its hub in Minneapolis and St. Paul largely to coastal destinations, including in Mexico and the Caribbean. It recently advertised one-way flights between Minneapolis and Orlando for $49.

If you are considering a low-cost carrier, check its route frequency. Often, budget carriers don’t fly to a destination daily, which could make it harder to rebook in case of bad weather or a mechanical delay.

Among the legacy carriers, American, Delta and United offer some form of basic economy tickets. Originally designed to compete with the likes of Spirit, these are nonrefundable, no-frills tickets.

They are also inflexible. While most standard economy tickets allow passengers to retain a credit for the airfare should fliers cancel before departure, basic economy fares restrict any changes. They also prohibit seat reservations and limit carry-ons.

Southwest Airlines grew on the promise of cheap flying, including no bag fees and open seating. But its policies now push it closer to the legacy carriers, including fees for checked bags and seats reserved in advance.

Southwest’s basic airfares have one perk that many lack: They are eligible for a flight credit if a flier cancels the reservation, though it is only good for six months from the initial date the reservation was booked.

Alaska Airlines has been making many upscale moves, including recently announcing lie-flat suites coming in 2028. But for frequent fliers in the West, it offers the subscription service Flight Pass. For $69 a month, members can fly round trip once every other month on Alaska flights in Arizona, California, Nevada and Utah (taxes and fees are extra). For $129, they can fly once a month.

Finding cheaper airfares draws on tried-and-true strategies, including being flexible on when and, if possible, where to go.

“If you can shift your dates or keep an open mind about where you go, you’ll find far more options than someone who’s locked into one specific route and one set weekend,” said Mr. Krauter of Going.com. “We recommend letting the deal decide. Instead of picking a destination and then checking prices, look at where fares are cheap from your airport first, then decide where to go.”

Going.com also recommends booking in what it calls the “Goldilocks window”: one to three months in advance for domestic flights, and two to eight months out for international. Peak travel periods, such as the holidays, expand those windows.

Airfares rise and fall with demand. The best fares are usually for flights on less busy days, such as Tuesdays and Saturdays.

“The days that you fly have a huge impact on how expensive your flight is,” said Ms. Berg of Hopper.

She added that returning home on the Sunday after Thanksgiving this year will cost on average $250 more than returning on Monday or Tuesday or even the Friday post-holiday.

Finally, consider alternative forms of payment. Now may be the time to break into your points bank or apply any credits from previous flights.

Follow New York Times Travel on Instagram and sign up for our Travel Dispatch newsletter to get expert tips on traveling smarter and inspiration for your next vacation. Dreaming up a future getaway or just armchair traveling? Check out our 52 Places to Go in 2026.

item.title: America’s Favorite Fruit Is Being Bruised by the Iran War
item.description:
The war in Iran has rippled through the global economy in many ways, pushing up prices for oil, fertilizer and other products. It has also created challenges for America’s most popular fruit: bananas.

The banana business has long been an underappreciated feat of logistics. It involves transporting a fragile and finicky fruit thousands of miles from the tropics, only to be sold for less than a quarter each. And it’s a business that is even trickier of late as the war raises the costs of fuel and other materials banana producers need.

That has put even more financial pressure on banana producers, who operate with thin margins and have little ability to raise prices. Compounding the industry’s problems are the threat of disease, climate change, tariffs and an exceptionally severe El Niño this year.

The banana might be America’s most unassuming fruit, a cheaply priced staple of smoothies and school cafeterias. It is the most consumed fruit in the United States, with Americans eating around 80 bananas a year, on average.

But bananas make little profit for grocery stores or the companies growing them. Instead, stores price them cheaply to draw shoppers in the door. The average price of bananas in the United States — about 65 cents a pound in August — has changed little over the last decade, despite rising costs.

“Everything is costing more money,” said Danny Dumas, a senior vice president at Del Monte North America. “If you ask me, it is a crisis.”

Even so, Del Monte, like the other major banana producers, Chiquita, Dole and Fyffes, continues to bring massive quantities of fruit to the United States.

In a port outside Philadelphia this summer, cranes and trucks busily unloaded hundreds of refrigerated containers from the Del Monte Spirit, a hulking ship that stretches two football fields long and had traveled more than 2,000 miles from Central America.

The ship, one of seven in Del Monte’s fleet, contained about 7 percent of the bananas that would be brought into the United States that week, supplying an area stretching from Iowa to North Carolina and Nova Scotia. The crew had just 40 hours to empty the ship’s cargo — millions of bananas from Guatemala and Costa Rica — before it would sail back for the next week’s pickup.

To understand the impact of the war, The New York Times traced the journey of a container of bananas from that ship over roughly 2,500 miles, from the plantation where it was grown to a Pennsylvania grocery store.

Some bananas on the Del Monte Spirit were grown in Tiquisate, a farm-dotted flood plain on the Pacific coast of Guatemala. Once carefully packed to avoid bruising, they were driven more than 250 miles in a refrigerated truck to Santo Tomás de Castilla, a port on Guatemala’s Caribbean coast.

The Spirit then carried them to Gloucester City, N.J., where Del Monte unloads up to 300,000 boxes of bananas a week. The company ships them directly to retailers or sends them to its own ripening facilities, which slowly increase the temperature and introduce ethylene gas so the bananas turn a perfect, unblemished yellow on your kitchen counter.

While many farmers and food sellers have seen costs increase because of the war, bananas have been hit harder because they are transported long distances and must be kept carefully refrigerated.

The price of diesel — needed to power Del Monte’s fleet of refrigerated trucks — has risen about 70 percent in the United States since the war started seven months ago, peaking at over $6 a gallon. Prices have also surged for the bunker fuel for Del Monte’s ships, and for the fuel for farmers’ irrigation systems in Central and South America.

The fertilizer that banana plantations depend on has also become more expensive, since much of it is made from natural gas coming from the Middle East. And the higher cost of shipping has spilled over into other products, like cardboard and plastic packaging and the chemicals that farmers spray on bananas to prevent disease.

Although the Trump administration has repeatedly pronounced the war with Iran over, the cease-fires have so far not held.

Transits out of the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz — which formerly helped to move about a third of the world’s fertilizer and a quarter of its seaborne oil — are still a small fraction of what they were. While more oil is flowing out of the Middle East than before, global oil prices have repeatedly breached $100 per barrel over the last seven months.

“Across the supply chain, everything depends on energy,” Mohammed Abbas, Del Monte’s president, said in an interview.

Del Monte grows some of its own bananas and buys others from farmers. Banana companies worry that higher prices may cause farmers to forgo fertilizer and disease-treating chemicals, resulting in a smaller crop next year. Some Central American farmers are already switching to pineapples.

Rising costs could also sap the industry’s ability to invest in disease-resistant varieties. The banana as Americans know it — a genetically homogeneous strain called Cavendish — is at risk from fungi and viruses that are spreading through South America.

While there are hundreds of varieties of bananas, ranging from the silvery-blue Ice Cream banana to the purplish Red Dacca, many Americans encounter only the Cavendish. Until the 1950s, Americans ate a variety called Gros Michel, a plumper, sweeter banana with a thick skin suited for shipping, and a flavor profile that lives on in banana-flavored candy.

But a fungus called Panama disease decimated the Gros Michel by the 1960s. Farmers turned to the Cavendish, first cultivated by an English gardener in the 1800s. Virtually all bananas consumed in the United States descend from that single English plant.

As farmers adapted, so did fungus. Another strain of Panama disease now targets Cavendish bananas in Southeast Asia and South America. It can survive in soil for decades, permanently wiping out farms.

Companies are quietly researching genetic alternatives in case the global supply collapses, an effort requiring significant investment. Del Monte declined to comment on its program.

Miguel Angel Morales, a small producer in northern Peru, said Panama disease had wiped out one in three banana-growing valleys in his region, forcing him and others to relocate their farms. The region produced 12 containers of bananas five years ago, but farmers now fill only one.

Stress from the war in Iran has compounded those problems. Mr. Morales said that his costs had jumped 25 to 30 percent this year, and that there was little support from banks or the government.

He had not yet raised his prices because annual contracts locked them in. Eventually, he thought, consumers in wealthier regions should pay more.

“If production costs increase, it’s logical that banana prices should increase, right?” he asked.

Yet an undisputed truth — at least among banana executives — is that the effort they put into their product has little relation to its price.

For decades, grocery stores have approached bananas as they do other “loss leaders” — pricing the fruit cheaply to get customers in the door. The industry structure, in which several companies compete to sell a largely identical product, also leaves banana producers with little power to raise their prices.

Banana companies have also developed highly efficient supply chains that shaved internal costs from farm to store — a strategy brutally perfected by the United Fruit Company, which turned large parts of Central America into company-run territory in the early 1900s.

The result is that the banana, despite being fragile and shipped long distances, is typically sold for as little as 15 cents each.

Adjusted for inflation, the average price of a pound of bananas in the United States has fallen roughly by half in the last 40 years. In the second quarter, Del Monte’s margin on bananas was just 2.3 percent.

“I always used to say that we are a nonprofit business,” said Juan Alarcon, the chief executive of Fyffes North America.

Banana companies also struggled last year with costs from tariffs, until the Trump administration exempted some food that is not locally grown in November.

Companies have also contended with a shortage of truck drivers, in part because the Trump administration stripped more than 30,000 drivers of commercial licenses.

The price at which many producers sell bananas is fixed by long-term contracts, some of which expire in December. But it’s not clear how much grocery stores will allow prices to rise.

Tom Stenzel, managing director of the Banana Association of North America, said it was “almost a mythology” among retailers that they couldn’t raise the price of bananas, the way they could for produce grown much closer to stores.

“I don’t want to throw my apple brothers under the bus,” Mr. Stenzel said, but apples are more expensive and take less effort to grow and ship. The banana industry’s ability to absorb costs is “at a breaking point,” he added.

“What else can you buy in a grocery store for 25 cents?” he asked.

Mitra Taj contributed reporting from Peru, and Jody García from Guatemala.

item.title: Duo Share Nobel in Economics for Work on Steering Through Booms and Busts
item.description:
The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences was awarded on Monday to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford, two American professors, for research that has helped guide policies aimed at reducing economic volatility.

Mr. Hall is a professor at Stanford University and Mr. Woodford is a professor of political economy at Columbia University. They were awarded the prize “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization,” the awarding committee said.

Mr. Hall studied consumer demand and spending to develop his models, while Mr. Woodford studied the supply side of the economy, looking at the price-setting behavior of companies. Their research has helped shape a framework for politicians, central banks and others to implement timely economic policies during upturns and downturns.

They will receive 12 million Swedish kronor, about $1.2 million, split equally between them.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said their work helped to inform fiscal and monetary policy measures, by governments and central banks, that reduced volatility in economies, so that there were milder peaks and troughs.

Because of their research, “we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” said John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences.

Mr. Hall and Mr. Woodford have revitalized so-called stabilization policy, which was pioneered by John Maynard Keynes, the early 20th-century British economist. This year’s prize winners developed models using microeconomic foundations, a bottom-up approach that considers how the decisions of individual households and businesses affect the economy as a whole.

By doing this, they showed the importance of how real-world behavior impacts policy and why it must be taken into account alongside broad economic variables like inflation and production. A critical aspect of their models rests on the idea that households and businesses make decisions based on what they believe will happen in the future. So when governments and policymakers communicate their economic plans, they can influence people’s expectations. That in itself can help steer the economy.

Mr. Woodford said on the phone at the news conference announcing the award that he was elated. “It’s a tremendous honor,” he said. “It’s a surprise but I feel very good about it.”

He said his work was intended to “improve the foundations for discussion of economic policy,” contributing to the management of the economy as well as the public’s understanding of the economy. He added that one of the main themes of his work was helping policymakers to appreciate that it was important to understand the behavior of individuals in the market: How they make decisions about spending and what they understand about future economic policy.

“One of the key goals of trying to develop an analytical framework was not simply to use it on people,” he said. “But to also talk to people about why the things that are being done are being done.”

Consider the immediate aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis, when central banks were scrambling to deal with an economic downturn. Policymakers quickly lowered interest rates but it wasn’t enough. Additional tools were developed, such as so-called forward guidance, in which central bankers made explicit statements about the likely future path of interest rates, Mr. Woodford said. “That was an important part of the policy response in the years from 2009 onward, and I think it did contribute to better stabilization,” he added.

Last year, Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt shared the award for their work on how innovation drives growth. The prize was given for research that explained the relationship between technological progress and sustained economic growth that has improved living standards, health and quality of life for people around the world.

The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Navi Pillay, a South African human rights lawyer and international judge, for what the committee called her efforts to uphold a system of international law that is increasingly under attack.

Anne Carson, a Canadian poet and essayist, was awarded the prize for literature for her “bold and inventive oeuvre.”

The prize for chemistry was awarded to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai for solving a longstanding mystery about mirror images in molecules.

Francis Halzen was awarded the prize in physics for pioneering a telescope that paved the way for a new kind of astronomy.

The prize for physiology or medicine was awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their discovery of a transformative neuroscience tool that may one day lead to a treatment for blindness.

item.title: I.M.F. Warns Mideast War Will Widen Gap Between Rich and Poor Countries
item.description:
Stubborn conflicts, high energy prices and rapid technological disruptions are deepening the divide between economic winners and losers across the globe, the International Monetary Fund warned on Tuesday in Bangkok.

Overall growth is lackluster but stable — 3.1 percent this year and 3.4 percent in 2027, the fund forecasts. But the average, it pointed out, “masks a reallocation of growth across economies.”

Countries, particularly low-income ones, that are dependent on oil imports and lack competitive tech-related sectors face an increased risk “that recent shocks will widen income gaps across and within countries.”

High energy and fuel prices will continue to take a bite out of households’ ability to pay their bills. The fund estimates that inflation will increase to 4.7 percent this year and 4.1 percent next year.

“A prolonged conflict in the Middle East could put additional pressures on inflation and slow down growth,” said Silvana Tenreyro, the fund’s chief economist. “The economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits,” she added.

The World Economic Outlook was released as top economic policymakers gathered in Bangkok this week for the annual meetings of the I.M.F. and the World Bank.

The unceasing economic shocks related to the ongoing war in Ukraine, conflict in the Middle East, President Trump’s tariffs and the collapse of a cooperative international economic order are roiling rich and poor countries as governments struggle to deal with conditions over which they often have limited control.

In France, the violent protests over decrepit schools and underpaid teachers are rooted in larger economic problems related to crushing public debt, high borrowing costs, elevated fuel prices and political discontent.

France was one of the few countries in the euro area whose outlook was downgraded from the fund’s previous report this year.

But the larger economic travails are dogging every nation.

Uncertainty is the watchword. There is little sign of a resolution in the Middle East as violence surged over the weekend with Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and strikes in Yemen.

Climate change is taking a toll. Intense heat and drought already disrupted supply chains and production this summer. Estimates of damage from El Niño could drag down global growth by trillions of dollars over time.

And speculation over the kind of upheaval artificial intelligence might cause ranges from supercharging productivity and profits to eradicating most jobs or even the human race.

The I.M.F. acknowledged that governments would be pressured to ease the burden of higher prices on households and businesses. But the fund’s economists sternly warned against overspending in a world of soaring debt and high borrowing costs, recommending assistance that is temporary and targeted.

In the United States, the fund is forecasting growth of 2.3 percent this year and next. Among countries that use the euro, growth is expected to reach only half that level. Britain does not fare much better, with estimated growth of 1.3 percent this year and a notch less next year.

In China, growth is expected to slow this year to 4.5 percent as the country strains to manage higher energy costs, a weak property sector and low levels of domestic consumption.

India is among the fastest-growing major economies, with growth projected to reach 7 percent this year. Other Southeast Asian countries are getting a boost from growth in data centers and other technology-related investment.

In the Middle East, Bahrain, Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar have all been gut-punched by the interruption of their oil and gas trade, and are expected to suffer double-digit drops in their total output this year, the fund said. They are expected to make up those losses next year as conditions get back to normal.

The forecast for Saudi Arabia, completed before the recent attacks, estimated that the country’s more diversified economy would contract 3.3 percent this year before growing 7.9 percent in 2027.

It will take another year before conditions in the Perisan Gulf return to prewar levels, the fund estimated. In the meantime, shortages are likely to persist even as oil production and delivery revive.

Poorer and developing nations will be most affected because they lack the resources to compete for limited supplies with richer countries.

“What’s happening is that every country has now suddenly figured out that energy security is national security,” said Ajay Banga, president of the World Bank.

Mr. Banga also focused on longer-term development issues. “We’ve got this demographic bulge coming,” he said. Over the next 12 to 15 years, roughly 1.2 billion young people in emerging economies will reach working age, but jobs won’t exist for most of them.

With foreign assistance from rich countries shrinking, Mr. Banga emphasized that private investment is the only way for emerging markets to spur economic growth and create jobs.

“It’s the math of development,” he said.
